extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military lawyers, court-martial members, and convening authorities
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing evidence, pleas, witnesses, record keeping, and corrections in courts-martial; guidance for conducting, revising, and authenticating military trials. Aimed at those who prepare, try, review, or correct court-martial proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to take testimony on guilty plea when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases in which the plea is guilty the court should take testimony where necessary to the comprehending of the facts and the doing of justice; the court should report such evidence to afford a full knowledge of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the accused pleads guilty, the court should receive and report evidence necessary to a full understanding of facts; this principle is rooted in early War Department orders (e.g., G. O. 23 of 1830).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to rebut evidence introduced after guilty plea
rubrics_metrics.description: Where evidence is introduced by the prosecution after a plea of guilty, the accused should be afforded an opportunity to offer rebutting evidence or evidence as to character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prosecution introduces new evidence after a guilty plea, the court must permit the accused to respond or present character witnesses (citing R. 13, 423, Feb., 1865).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider plea and statement/confession together
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, in connection with a plea of guilty, a statement or confession (oral or written) is interposed by the accused, both plea and statement should be considered together by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the statement indicates evidence exists that will constitute a defense or reduce culpability, the court should call upon or permit the judge advocate to obtain and introduce such evidence if practicable (R. 14, 585 and 596, June, 1865, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements inconsistent with plea may control
rubrics_metrics.description: If an accused who pleads guilty makes an oral or written statement inconsistent with the plea, the statement rather than the plea may be regarded as the intelligent act of the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the court should counsel the accused to plead not guilty or direct such plea to be entered and proceed to trial with the judge advocate introducing proof as under an ordinary plea of not guilty (R. 8, 274; R. 6, 357, 370).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion to allow material testimony after formal close but before finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may, in its discretion, allow the introduction by either side of material testimony after the case has been formally closed but before a finding has been reached, if justice requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such admissions should be exceptional and the offering party must show good reason for not having produced the testimony earlier (R. 12, 401; R. 17, 398; R. 31, 35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularity of admitting evidence after finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The admission of evidence after reaching a finding and after receiving evidence of previous convictions is highly irregular and generally improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the court may reconsider or change findings/sentences while proceedings remain in its possession, it should not reopen the case to hear new evidence after a finding of guilt or not guilty (C. 18764, May 5, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: General pardon or amnesty affects jurisdiction—must be noticed
rubrics_metrics.description: A court is bound to take judicial notice, as affecting its jurisdiction, of a general pardon or amnesty; an individual pardon must be pleaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a general amnesty applies to the charged offense (e.g., amnesty proclamation of March 11, 1865), the court lacks jurisdiction and the trial is illegal (C. 1274, Apr., 1895).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration to duty as plea in bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A plea of restoration to duty by competent authority without trial, under Army Regulations, is in the nature of a plea of a constructive pardon and is a good special plea in bar of trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, proceeding to trial on the general issue waives this plea (B. Jf.9, 94, May, 1885).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive previous punishment not a bar to trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior reduction in rank, confinement in arrest, or required labor under custody—even if in excess of authority—does not constitute a legal plea in bar to trial for the charged offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such prior treatment is relevant only to consideration of the quantum of punishment upon conviction (R. 47, 242, July, 1883).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form objections must be raised by special plea or motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to the charges or specifications in matters of form (inartificial, indefinite, redundant, misnaming, misdescription, insufficient allegations of time/place) should be taken advantage of by special pleas in the nature of pleas in abatement or by motion to strike out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objections should be raised early so that amendable errors can be corrected on the spot by the judge advocate; if not taken, they are generally waived by plea of guilty or not guilty (numerous citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misnomer or misdescription waived by unobjected plea
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, without preliminary objection, the accused pleads guilty or not guilty to a specification in which he is incorrectly named or described, such plea will be regarded as an admission of identity and he cannot later object on account of misnomer or misdescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity affects witness competency and proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: An insane person is no more competent as a witness before a court-martial than at common law; if indications of insanity are developed by the accused during trial, the court should suspend proceedings and report to the convening authority, adjourning to await orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person shown to be insane should be stricken out on motion (R. 50, 270; R. 33, 661).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict exclusion of judge advocate from closed sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation excluding the judge advocate from closed sessions of a court-martial must be strictly complied with; no discretion to except or permit presence is contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply would probably vitiate proceedings; if noncompliance is found and the court has not arrived at a finding, the court should be dissolved and a new trial ordered (C. 1637; C. 12962; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge advocate withdrawal not required for reading findings/sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The act requiring withdrawal of the judge advocate for closed sessions does not apply to meetings of the court to hear read the record of the findings and sentence, such proceedings being no part of the trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may sit in closed session before being sworn
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial may sit in closed session before it has been sworn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused with statements disclaiming intent to desert—investigate
rubrics_metrics.description: When an accused charged with desertion pleads guilty but makes a statement disclaiming any intention to abandon service, the court should not fairly convict of desertion without investigation and should induce change to not guilty or direct plea and take evidence showing actual offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative citation: R. 26, 562, May, 1868; comparable practice for distinguishing elements in larceny or other offenses (IX I 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie votes are negative; majority required for affirmative
rubrics_metrics.description: A tie vote upon any proposition submitted to the court is equivalent to a negative vote; a majority vote is necessary for an affirmative determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If vote ties on objection to testimony, the objection is not sustained; if tied on a proposed finding or form of sentence, it is not adopted (R. 31, 511; C. £003).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polling of court-martial unknown/irregular
rubrics_metrics.description: The polling of a court-martial, in the manner of a jury or otherwise, is a proceeding wholly unknown to military law and is irregular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An officer demanding polling of a court-martial (e.g., after adverse ruling) acted irregularly and disrespectfully (R. 34, 444).

rubrics_metrics.name: No individual protest by minority entered on record
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a majority of members have decided, no individual of the minority is entitled to have a protest made by himself entered upon the record; the conclusions of the court are determined by the vote of the majority (except death sentences require two-thirds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protests by minority cannot be appended to the record on a separate paper (R. 11, 203; R. 25, 542; R. 36, 264).

rubrics_metrics.name: President cannot adjourn against majority vote
rubrics_metrics.description: For the president of a court-martial to assume to adjourn the court against the vote of the majority is an unauthorized act and a grave irregularity, subjecting him to charges under the sixty-second article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjournment sine die has no power to dissolve court
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjournment sine die has no more legal effect than a simple adjournment; it does not dissolve the court which cannot terminate its own existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After adjournment sine die the court may reassemble without reconvening by the convening authority and proceed as if not adjourned; it may also be reconvened by the convening authority for reconsideration (R. 21, 679; R. 55, 208; C. 5651^).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication of record by president and judge advocate suffices when no material proceedings after sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are no material proceedings after the sentence, the subscription of the sentence by the president and judge advocate will constitute a sufficient authentication of the record as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If president or judge advocate changed pending trial, the last one serving at close should sign; a judge advocate appointed after conclusion would not be competent to authenticate (R. 19, 616; R. 29, 604; C. 5230).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing authority may reassemble court to correct record defects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reviewing authority deems the forwarded record to exhibit errors, omissions or defects capable of being supplied or remedied by the court, the court may properly be reconvened by order of the reviewing officer for the purpose of correcting the record, provided correction is practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of correctable defects: inadequate/irregular sentence, finding not authorized by evidence, omission to prefix convening order, missing signatures, incorrect statement as to members present, failure to record plea, finding or sentence. There is generally no limit to reconvenings for revision, though not often reassembled twice if declined once (multiple citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassembling order should specify particulars to be revised
rubrics_metrics.description: The order reassembling the court should indicate the particular or particulars as to which a revision or correction is desired, or refer to accompanying papers setting forth the supposed omission or defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to make the proposed correction is in the discretion of the court; the reviewing authority cannot compel the court to make it (R. 11, 93; R. 7, 112; R. 24, 435).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum membership for legal correction
rubrics_metrics.description: A correction can be made only by a legal court; at least five of the members who acted upon the trial must be present when reconvened to correct the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fewer members at reassembling than at trial is immaterial provided five are present; the judge advocate should be present (R. 35, 656; R. 1, 487).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused's presence not generally necessary at revision
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally not necessary or desirable that the accused be present at a revision; however, where any possible injustice may result from his absence, he should be required or permitted to be present, and with counsel if preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defect to be corrected consists in omission to set forth a special plea or objection by the accused, his presence may be desirable; clerical errors do not generally call for his presence (R. 9, 653).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court reconvened for revision cannot take new testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial reconvened for revision of its proceedings is not empowered to take or receive testimony during that proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections must be made by act of the court, not by erasure or indorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments or corrections can only be made by the court when duly reconvened for the purpose and must be the act of the court as such; corrections by president, other member, or judge advocate independently, or by erasure/interlineation, are unauthorized and grave irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record of the correction must be made in the formal proceedings upon the revision and must refer to the page/part where omission occurs; the original part must remain precisely as it stands (R. 28, 304; R. 2, 97; R. 11, 93; R. 16, 202; R. 34, 416).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indorsement by judge advocate cannot substitute for regular amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: An indorsement by the trial judge advocate cannot be received in place of a regular amendment of the record by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: No correction possible if court dissolved or cannot be reconvened
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the court has been dissolved or cannot practically be reconvened by reason of casualty or exigency of service, no correction of its proceedings is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of dissolution effective only once officially known
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial is not legally dissolved until officially informed of an order dissolving it; proceedings after the date of an order dissolving it but before official notice are regular and valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an order dissolving forthwith has been officially received and taken effect, a subsequent revoking order is futile; the court must be reconvened as a new tribunal to act (R. 49, 160; P. 32, 29).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desertion does not render witness incompetent
rubrics_metrics.description: Desertion is not a felony and does not render a witness incompetent at common law or before a court-martial; loss of citizenship upon conviction of desertion does not affect competency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although competent, where such a person is proposed as material witness for the prosecution in an important case it may be desirable to remit unexecuted portion of his sentence (R. 61, 254).

rubrics_metrics.name: Members and judge advocate may testify but generally undesirable
rubrics_metrics.description: The president or any member of a court-martial, as also the judge advocate, may legally give testimony before the court; however it is generally undesirable that they do so except perhaps on matters of good character or record of the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony by a member does not affect validity of proceedings even if only five members remain (R. 2, 581; R. 7, 202; R. 11, 299).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of witness from list not fatal; better practice to list
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an objection to the competency of a witness that his name is not on the list of witnesses appended to the charges when served; the prosecutor is not obliged to furnish any list, though it is better practice to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When list is furnished, prosecution may still use other witnesses; unexpected witness testimony may be grounds for accused to request further time for preparation (R. 25, 350).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wife of prosecuting witness is competent; wife of accused generally not
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to admit testimony of the wife of a prosecuting witness as incompetent is erroneous; conversely, the wife of an accused party generally could not properly be admitted as a witness for or against him under common law principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited rulings: R. 43, 106; C. 17946; R. 30, 672; R. 47, 521. Exceptions and nuances noted (e.g., cases where wife's testimony immaterial or joint charges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity as witness competency requires clear proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who is insane at the time is incompetent as a witness; an objection on this ground should not be allowed unless sustained by clear proof, as one is presumed sane until proven otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special care with child witnesses—suspend and instruct
rubrics_metrics.description: Where conviction rests mainly on testimony of a very young child (e.g., 8 years old), the competency of the witness may be doubtful and the trial should have been suspended to instruct the child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative: rape conviction case (R. 50, 37, Feb., 1886).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military courts generally follow civilian competency rules where apposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules governing competency of witnesses before U.S. criminal courts and the States are generally (though not always) followed in courts-martial practice where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused entitled to have material witnesses summoned
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where testimony would be merely cumulative and add nothing, the accused is generally entitled to have any and all material witnesses summoned to testify on his behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt obedience to a summons is incumbent on all witnesses; superior officers should not place obstacles to the attendance of summoned inferiors (R. 33, 100; R. 43, 341; C. 17212; C. 17666).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance of extremely high officials rarely required
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused can rarely demand attendance as a witness of a chief of staff, President, or Secretary of War; if necessary and not obtainable by deposition, the court may adjourn to a convenient point to secure attendance without detriment to public interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoenas may be served by military or civil persons but preferably by military
rubrics_metrics.description: A summons may legally be served by either a military or a civil person, but will generally preferably be served by an officer or noncommissioned officer of the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge advocate or officer is not authorized to employ a U.S. marshal or civil official and commit the U.S. to pay fees, except limited ratifications where economical and effectual (R. 43, 284; R. 37, 570; P. 32, 365; C. 5549; C. 13418).

rubrics_metrics.name: No authorized fee for subpoena service; limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fee or compensation established or authorized to be paid by statute or regulation for service of subpoenas or attendance of witnesses before military courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither commanding officer nor judge advocate is authorized to employ a civilian for such service or to obligate U.S.; in rare cases where civilian employment was necessary and economical, reasonable compensation has been allowed out of Army contingencies (P. 32, 365; C. 5519; C. 13418).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoenas for foreign-resident witnesses transmitted through State Department
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpoenas for witnesses residing in foreign territory should be transmitted through the Department of State for service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness cannot unilaterally leave when found material
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness cannot discharge or relieve himself from attendance on the ground that his testimony is immaterial; it is for the court to judge materiality and unless determined incompetent or inadmissible he must remain and stand examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In civil practice such an act would be contempt; witness should remain until informed by court or judge advocate that attendance is no longer required (B. 39, 354).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege against self-incrimination is personal
rubrics_metrics.description: The common-law privilege of a witness to refuse to answer a question the answer to which may incriminate him is a personal one which the witness may exercise or waive; it is not for the judge advocate or accused to object or for the court to exclude the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where witness is ignorant of right, the court may advise him; if military witness refuses to answer on privilege but court decides question not incriminating and orders answer, refusal thereafter may render him liable to charges under article 62 (R. 11, 220; R. 34, 242).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special protection for cadet witnesses re self-incrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: A cadet witness at a Military Academy trial could refuse to testify to facts which would tend to incriminate him; requiring such testimony over objection was erroneous and the court should instruct the witness of his rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 38, 194, Jan., 1890; emphasizes witness-only privilege and need for court instruction if ignorant of rights.
